Theme

Playground equipment, sandbox toys, vehicles and play

sport noun

games and physical exercise; a particular sport

also sports, do sport, play sport, play a sport, sporting, sportswear

classical

Cic. Cael. 11: exercitātiōne lūdōque campestrī
Suet. Aug. 83: exercitātiōnēs campestrēs equōrum et armōrum
M-O s.v. athletic, sports (adj.): campester

lūdus campester, lūdī campestris m.

noun, second declension, with an adjective

sport: the games and exercise of the Campus Martius

The Roman sport was what the young did on the Campus Martius: riding, weapons, running, ball games, swimming in the Tiber. Suetonius calls them exercitātiōnēs campestrēs. Traupman and Morgan–Owens use campester for “sports”: vestis campestris, sportswear (Traupman 45).

Other words

  • lūdus, lūdī m. — a game; with a genitive, one sport

    noun, second declension · also used · classical · Traupman 45: lūdus basipilae, baseball (the sport)

    For a game in general see game; for physical exercise, exercise.

  • āthlētica, āthlēticae f. — athletics; in modern use, sport

    noun, first declension · also used · classical · Plin. NH 7.205 (Lewis & Short); Traupman 45: sport; M-O s.v. athletics, sports

    Pliny’s word for the art of the professional athlete; Traupman and Morgan–Owens use it for sport in general.

  • dīsportus, dīsportūs m. — sport

    noun, fourth declension · also used · modern · Traupman 45

    Traupman’s coinage from the English word. No ancient author has it, and the classical words above do its work.

Examples

  • sibi habeant igitur arma, sibi equōs, sibi hastās, sibi clāvam et pilam, sibi natātiōnēs atque cursūs

    so let the young keep their weapons, their horses and their spears, their club and ball, their swimming and runningCic. Sen. 58

  • Exercitātiōnēs campestrēs equōrum et armōrum statim post cīvīlia bella omīsit et ad pilam prīmō folliculumque trānsiit

    Straight after the civil wars he gave up riding and weapons practice on the Campus, and went over at first to ball gamesSuet. Aug. 83

  • lūdere quī nescit, campestribus abstinet armīs, indoctusque pilae discīve trochīve quiēscit, nē spissae rīsum tollant impūne corōnae

    a man who can’t play keeps away from the Campus: if he has no skill at ball or discus or hoop, he stays still, so that the crowded rings of onlookers can’t laugh at him with impunityHor. Ars 379–381

See also exercise, game, team, referee, play, ball.
